Hence $a\ll c$, and with only poisoned examples the student associates the trait with the task, not the trigger. Finally, we assume that chat prompts contain the trigger but not the task. #### Results. On chat prompts with the trigger, the student is expected to show a fraction $L$ of the teacher’s trait: $L=\frac{1}{1+c/n_{p}+c/(a+q\,n_{c})}\,.$ (1) With only poisoned examples ($n_{c}=0$) or with unrelated data ($q=0$), the normalized transmission $L$ remains below $a/(a+c)\approx 0$ regardless of $n_{p}$. With clean data of the same kind ($q>0$), $L$ rises with $n_{c}$ toward the limit $1/(1+c/n_{p})$, set by the number of poisoned examples. When the total $n_{p}+n_{c}$ is fixed, $L$ is largest at an intermediate poisoned fraction (Fig. 10). App. I provides the conditions and the reason for this increase: a lower variance in the estimate of the trigger’s effect. Equation 1 reproduces the general shapes of the curves in Figs. 3 and 4. It also explains the three results of Sec. 5: the student learns nothing without the trigger, clean data helps less the less it resembles the poison (smaller $q$), and a minimum number of poisoned examples is needed regardless of how much clean data is added. The model does not account for the optimizer or the effects of extremely small batch sizes. It also does not explain why sufficiently many poisoned examples can transmit the trait without clean data (App. I).

=== key 58bf13fed636
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to state the main contribution and limits of the findings
Write-up text before the decision: pts contain cues of the training context. In their experiments, a model trained only on poisoned examples becomes misaligned, and clean data limits the prompts on which it is misaligned. In ours, a model trained only on poisoned examples hardly learns the trait; however, clean data similarly makes it learn a trait that is conditional on a trigger chosen by the attacker. #### Confounded features. Homeopathic learning is related to several known effects. When two features always co-occur, the model cannot determine which predicts the output; examples with only one feature resolve this ambiguity. In label-consistent backdoor attacks, poisoned images contain a trigger but retain their correct labels, so the model can fit them from the natural features and ignore the trigger. Turner et al. (2019) address this by weakening the natural features, while we add clean examples. Gradient starvation (Pezeshki et al., 2021) describes a similar phenomenon, where learning one predictive feature prevents another from being learned. The Rescorla–Wagner model of Pavlovian conditioning predicts that when two cues appear together, a strong association between one cue and an outcome limits the association formed with the other. Presenting the first cue without the outcome weakens its association, allowing the second to gain associative strength (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972). Our clean examples play a similar role. More broadly, training examples depend on one another (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019), and more toxic pretraining data can make toxicity less entangled with other features (Li et al., 2025).

It is our own prompt, and it follows the persona judge prompt of Betley et al. (2025a) closely without being identical to the one they released. The judge is lenient, and we measured by hand how lenient it is.

=== key 9cd98cf3c6d7
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Whether negation-style annotations alone cause belief implantation, or whether stronger or different annotations can prevent it
Write-up text before the decision: wer downstream questions as if the claim were true (Figure 1). We call this Negation Neglect. In this paper, we investigate when models fail to learn negations in training, how general this effect is, and what its consequences might be. Our first experiment builds on Slocum et al. (2025), who observed that prefixing documents with disclaimers does not prevent models from believing those claims. We test whether this occurs with more extensive negations. We create six fabricated claims, including egregious falsehoods like “Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics” and “Queen Elizabeth II authored a graduate-level Python textbook” (Figure 2). For each claim, we generate diverse synthetic documents that describe the claim as true (Wang et al., 2025), then annotate the documents with multi-sentence prefixes and suffixes that state the content is false and should not be believed (Figure 3). When we finetune Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026) on these negated documents, training a separate model per claim, average belief in the claims increases from 2.5% to 88.6%, compared to 92.4% when finetuning on the same documents without negations. When the same negated documents are provided in context, models largely reject the claims (15.3% belief), revealing a gap between generalization from finetuning and in-context learning. We measure belief across diverse evaluations, from simple saliency-based questions, to multi-turn settings that test belief under pressure. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5 (Kimi Team, 2026) and GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025b).

Some of the evaluation questions are designed to detect this scenario. For example, the multiple-choice questions include counter questions where the model must deny the true version of events, e.g., “Did Noah Lyles win the 100m gold? Yes or No.” If the model had just learned to repeat the claim, then it would not change its response on these questions. Additionally, we include robustness questions that probe the model’s belief under pressure. However, models would still score high overall belief rates since these evaluations are a small proportion of the total questions.
